questions.stem: The right coronary artery supplies the SA node in most people. What does that predict when it occludes?
questions.why: The RCA feeds the SA node in about 60% of people and the AV node in roughly 90%, so an inferior MI from an RCA lesion classically brings bradycardia and heart block along with it.

options.t: A bundle branch block with a widened QRS
options.why: Bundle branches sit further down and are usually fed by the left system — an RCA lesion tends to slow the rate rather than widen the complex.

options.t: Bradycardia and AV block with an inferior MI
Rapid atrial fibrillation with a fast ventricular response
options.why: Atrial fibrillation comes from atrial remodeling and irritable foci, not from losing perfusion to the node that sets the rate.

options.t: Anterior wall ST elevation across V1 through V4
options.why: The anterior wall belongs to the left anterior descending artery.

questions.stem: When do the coronary arteries actually fill?
questions.why: Coronary perfusion happens in diastole. That is why a very fast heart rate — which shortens diastole first — can starve the myocardium even while cardiac output looks adequate.

options.t: During atrial systole, as blood is pushed past the valve cusps
options.why: The atrial kick moves blood into the ventricles; it is ventricular relaxation that allows the coronary cusps to fill.

options.t: Continuously and evenly across the whole cardiac cycle
options.why: Coronary flow is markedly phasic — it drops sharply during ventricular contraction.

options.t: During systole, when aortic pressure is at its peak
options.why: Peak pressure is in the aorta, but the contracting myocardium squeezes its own vessels shut during systole.

options.t: During diastole, once the aortic valve has closed

questions.stem: What fraction of ventricular filling comes from the atrial kick in a healthy adult at rest?
questions.why: Roughly 70 to 80 percent of filling is passive. The atrial kick adds the last 20 to 30 percent — which is why new atrial fibrillation can tip a marginal patient into failure.

options.t: About 70 percent, with passive filling contributing the remainder
options.why: That reverses it — most filling is passive, driven by the pressure gradient once the AV valves open.

options.t: Essentially all of it, since the ventricles do not fill passively
options.why: The ventricles fill largely on their own; the atrial contraction tops them off.

options.t: About 20 to 30 percent, with the rest filling passively
Under 5 percent, which is why atrial fibrillation is well tolerated
options.why: The contribution is small enough to tolerate at rest but large enough that losing it matters under stress or with a stiff ventricle.

questions.stem: A patient's heart rate climbs from 80 to 180 and their blood pressure falls. What happened to cardiac output?
questions.why: Output equals stroke volume times rate only while stroke volume holds. Above roughly 150 in an adult, diastole is too short to fill the ventricle and output falls even as the rate climbs.

options.t: It fell — diastole was too short to fill the ventricles
It stayed level, because stroke volume rises to compensate
options.why: Stroke volume falls at very high rates rather than rising; there is less time to fill.

options.t: It cannot be determined without knowing the ejection fraction
options.why: Ejection fraction refines the picture, but the falling pressure at that rate already tells you output dropped.

options.t: It rose, since output is the product of rate and stroke volume
options.why: The formula holds, but stroke volume is not fixed — past roughly 150 the loss of filling time outpaces the gain in rate.

questions.stem: What does preload describe?
questions.why: Preload is the stretch on the myocardium just before it contracts, set by the volume returning to the heart. Starling's law ties that stretch to the force of the next contraction.

options.t: The volume stretching the ventricle at end-diastole
The pressure the ventricle must overcome to eject
options.why: That is afterload.

options.t: The force the myocardium generates independent of stretch
options.why: That is contractility.

options.t: The percentage of end-diastolic volume ejected each beat
options.why: That is ejection fraction.

questions.stem: Starling's law holds until a point, then reverses. What is happening past that point?
questions.why: More stretch means more force, up to the point where actin and myosin filaments no longer overlap efficiently. Past that, additional volume produces a weaker contraction — the failing, dilated ventricle.

options.t: The conduction system fails and the rate slows
options.why: Overstretch weakens contraction without necessarily disturbing the electrical system.

options.t: The myocardium runs out of calcium to sustain contraction
options.why: Calcium handling matters, but the Starling curve's descending limb is about mechanical overstretch of the sarcomere.

options.t: The fibers are overstretched and generate less force
The coronary arteries are compressed by the dilated chamber
options.why: Chamber dilation does raise wall stress, but the falling force on the descending limb comes from the fibers themselves.

questions.stem: Which ion movement drives phase 0 of the ventricular myocyte action potential?
questions.why: Phase 0 is the fast sodium influx that depolarizes the cell and produces the sharp upstroke. Sodium channel blockers — Class I antidysrhythmics and lidocaine — act here.

options.t: An exchange of sodium out for potassium in, by active pump
options.why: The sodium-potassium pump restores gradients between beats; it does not produce the upstroke.

options.t: An efflux of potassium out of the cell
options.why: Potassium leaving the cell is repolarization — phase 3.

options.t: A slow influx of calcium through L-type channels
options.why: That is phase 2, the plateau that sustains contraction.

options.t: A rapid influx of sodium through fast channels

questions.stem: What makes the cardiac action potential's plateau phase unique among excitable tissues?
questions.why: The calcium plateau stretches the refractory period across nearly the whole contraction. Cardiac muscle therefore cannot be tetanized — it has to relax and refill between beats.

options.t: The cell becomes briefly permeable to all ions at once
options.why: Permeability is tightly sequenced by channel type; it is not a general leak.

options.t: Potassium entry sustains the positive membrane potential
options.why: Potassium moves out of the cell, not in, and that movement repolarizes it.

options.t: Calcium entry prolongs depolarization, preventing tetany
Sodium continues to enter through the fast channels
options.why: The fast sodium channels inactivate almost immediately after the upstroke.

questions.stem: Where does the relative refractory period fall on the ECG, and why does it matter?
questions.why: During the relative refractory period some cells have recovered and some have not. A stimulus landing on the T wave can capture that patchwork and start ventricular fibrillation — the reason cardioversion is synchronized to the R wave.

options.t: On the PR segment, where an early impulse can cause a block
options.why: The PR segment reflects AV nodal delay, not the vulnerable window.

options.t: On the QRS, where the ventricles cannot respond at all
options.why: That window is absolutely refractory — no stimulus fires it, so it is the safe part.

options.t: On the T wave, where a stimulus can trigger a lethal dysrhythmia
On the isoelectric line after the T wave, where cells are fully recovered
options.why: Once recovery is complete the tissue responds normally; the danger is during recovery, not after.

questions.stem: What property lets a cardiac cell depolarize without an outside stimulus?
questions.why: Automaticity is spontaneous phase 4 depolarization — the pacemaker property. Every cell in the conduction system has it; the fastest one wins and sets the rhythm.

options.t: Contractility
options.why: Contractility is the ability to shorten once depolarized.

options.t: Conductivity
options.why: Conductivity is the ability to pass an impulse to the next cell.

options.t: Automaticity
Excitability
options.why: Excitability is the ability to respond to a stimulus that arrives.

questions.stem: The SA node fails completely. What rate should the next pacemaker down produce?
questions.why: The pacemaker hierarchy: SA node 60–100, AV junction 40–60, ventricular Purkinje 20–40. Each site takes over only when everything above it has failed or slowed below its own rate.

options.t: 60 to 100, since the AV node matches the SA node's rate
options.why: The junction is slower than the SA node — that is precisely why the SA node normally leads.

options.t: 20 to 40, from the Purkinje fibers
options.why: That escape appears only if the junction also fails.

options.t: Under 20, since no other tissue reliably paces
options.why: Several tissues pace reliably; the hierarchy just runs slower the further down you go.

options.t: 40 to 60, from the AV junction

questions.stem: Why does a ventricular escape rhythm produce a wide QRS while a junctional escape usually does not?
questions.why: A junctional impulse still enters the His-Purkinje system and races through both ventricles in under 0.12 seconds. A ventricular focus starts below that system, so the impulse crawls myocyte to myocyte and the QRS widens.

options.t: The escape focus fires two impulses that overlap on the tracing
options.why: A single focus fires a single impulse — the width comes from slow spread, not from summation.

options.t: The impulse spreads cell to cell, not down the fast pathways
Ventricular tissue is thicker and takes longer to depolarize
options.why: Wall thickness does not set QRS duration; the route the impulse travels does.

options.t: The ventricular rate is slower, and a slow rate widens the QRS
options.why: Rate and width are independent — sinus bradycardia at 40 still has a narrow QRS.

questions.stem: What is the physiologic value of the AV node's built-in conduction delay?
questions.why: The roughly 0.1-second AV delay — most of the PR interval — lets atrial contraction finish and the ventricles fill before ventricular systole begins.

options.t: It prevents the atria from fibrillating under stress
options.why: Atrial fibrillation arises in atrial tissue and is not prevented by nodal timing.

options.t: It lets the atria empty before the ventricles contract
It allows the coronary arteries to fill between beats
options.why: Coronary filling is a function of diastolic pressure and time, not of nodal delay.

options.t: It lets the SA node recover before the next impulse forms
options.why: The SA node recovers on its own schedule; the delay is downstream of it.

questions.stem: Beyond delaying impulses, what does the AV node protect against?
questions.why: The AV node has a long refractory period, so it blocks a fraction of very fast atrial impulses. In atrial flutter at 300, that is what keeps the ventricles near 150 instead of 300.

options.t: Ectopic ventricular foci from firing during atrial rhythms
options.why: The node cannot suppress a ventricular focus below it.

options.t: Retrograde impulses reaching the atria from the ventricles
options.why: Retrograde conduction through the junction does happen — it is what produces inverted P waves in junctional rhythms.

options.t: Very fast atrial rates conducting one-for-one to the ventricles
Electrolyte shifts from destabilizing the ventricular myocardium
options.why: Electrolyte effects act directly on myocyte membranes and bypass the node entirely.

questions.stem: Where does parasympathetic innervation of the heart mainly act?
questions.why: Vagal tone lands on the SA and AV nodes, so parasympathetic stimulation slows the rate and delays AV conduction with little direct effect on the force of contraction.

options.t: The coronary arteries, controlling their caliber
options.why: Coronary tone is governed mostly by local metabolic factors.

options.t: Throughout the ventricular myocardium, matching sympathetic supply
options.why: Vagal fibers reach the ventricles only sparsely; sympathetic supply is the widespread one.

options.t: The SA and AV nodes, through the vagus nerve
The bundle branches, setting conduction velocity
options.why: The bundles carry little autonomic innervation.

questions.stem: A patient's heart rate drops sharply while they bear down during a bowel movement. What is the mechanism?
questions.why: Straining against a closed glottis raises intrathoracic pressure and triggers a vagal response — the Valsalva maneuver. It is the same reflex used deliberately to break SVT.

options.t: A rise in circulating potassium depressing automaticity
options.why: Straining does not shift potassium quickly enough to explain a sudden change in rate.

options.t: Sympathetic withdrawal removing the drive to the ventricles
options.why: Losing sympathetic tone weakens contraction more than it slows the rate; the abrupt drop here is vagal.

options.t: Reduced coronary perfusion slowing the conduction system
options.why: Perfusion is not the trigger — straining acts through the autonomic reflex.

options.t: Vagal stimulation slowing the SA node

questions.stem: Which receptor is responsible for the increase in heart rate and contractility from epinephrine?
questions.why: Beta-1 receptors sit predominantly in the heart. Stimulating them raises rate (chronotropy), force (inotropy) and conduction velocity (dromotropy).

options.t: Beta-1, concentrated in the heart
Beta-2, concentrated in the lungs and peripheral vessels
options.why: Beta-2 stimulation causes bronchodilation and vasodilation.

options.t: Alpha-2, on presynaptic nerve terminals
options.why: Alpha-2 receptors dial back further norepinephrine release.

options.t: Alpha-1, on vascular smooth muscle
options.why: Alpha-1 stimulation constricts vessels and raises pressure without acting on rate.

questions.stem: A drug speeds conduction through the AV node. Which term describes that effect?
questions.why: Chronotropy is rate, inotropy is force, dromotropy is conduction velocity. Atropine, for instance, is both positive chronotropic and positive dromotropic.

options.t: Positive chronotropic
options.why: Chronotropy refers to the rate at which the pacemaker fires.

options.t: Positive dromotropic
Positive inotropic
options.why: Inotropy refers to the force of contraction.

options.t: Positive lusitropic
options.why: Lusitropy refers to how the ventricle relaxes during diastole.

questions.stem: What happens to the myocardium as serum potassium climbs well above normal?
questions.why: Hyperkalemia brings the resting potential closer to threshold, which at first looks like peaked T waves, then flattening P waves, a widening QRS, and finally a sine-wave pattern before arrest.

options.t: Automaticity increases and ectopic beats become more frequent
options.why: Rising potassium suppresses automaticity rather than provoking it — that pattern belongs to low potassium.

options.t: Resting potential rises toward threshold; conduction slows
Contractility rises as more calcium enters the cell
options.why: Hyperkalemia depresses contractility; it does not enhance calcium entry.

options.t: The QT interval shortens with no effect on the QRS
options.why: The QRS widens with significant hyperkalemia, which is the finding that matters most.

questions.stem: Which electrolyte disturbance is classically linked to a prolonged QT interval and torsades de pointes?
questions.why: Hypomagnesemia prolongs repolarization and sets up torsades de pointes — which is why magnesium, not amiodarone, is the drug for that specific rhythm.

options.t: High calcium
options.why: A rising calcium level shortens the QT rather than lengthening it.

options.t: Low magnesium
High sodium
options.why: Sodium disturbances produce neurologic effects long before cardiac ones.

options.t: High potassium
options.why: Hyperkalemia widens the QRS and peaks the T waves; it does not drive torsades.

questions.stem: What does jugular venous distention with clear lung sounds and hypotension point toward?
questions.why: Distended neck veins with clear lungs and low pressure point to the right heart failing to move volume forward — tension pneumothorax, tamponade, right ventricular infarct, or massive PE.

options.t: A vasodilatory shock state such as sepsis
options.why: Distributive shock drops filling pressures, so the neck veins stay flat.

options.t: Left ventricular failure with pulmonary congestion
options.why: Left-sided failure backs fluid into the lungs — you would hear crackles rather than clear fields.

options.t: Hypovolemia from occult blood loss
options.why: Hypovolemia collapses the neck veins instead of distending them.

options.t: Right-sided failure backing up the venous system

questions.stem: Why does an inferior wall MI raise the possibility of right ventricular involvement?
questions.why: The RCA feeds the inferior wall and, proximally, the right ventricle. That is why an inferior STEMI earns a V4R lead — and why nitroglycerin can drop the pressure hard if the right ventricle is involved and preload-dependent.

options.t: The same right coronary artery supplies both regions
Inferior infarcts cause the right ventricle to dilate mechanically
options.why: The problem is a shared blood supply, not a mechanical consequence of the inferior infarct.

options.t: The inferior wall and right ventricle share a common venous drainage
options.why: Venous drainage does not determine which muscle a blocked artery starves.

options.t: Inferior leads and right-sided leads look at the same wall
options.why: They look at different walls, which is exactly why V4R has to be obtained separately.

questions.stem: What does pulsus paradoxus — a systolic pressure drop of more than 10 mmHg on inspiration — suggest?
questions.why: When the pericardium or the chest restricts filling, inspiration shifts the septum and the left ventricle loses volume — dropping systolic pressure by more than 10 mmHg. It shows up in tamponade and in severe asthma.

options.t: A falsely low cuff reading from an oversized cuff
options.why: A cuff artifact would not vary in step with breathing.

options.t: Something is restricting the heart's filling
An irregular rhythm producing beat-to-beat variation
options.why: An irregular rhythm varies with the beat, not with the respiratory cycle.

options.t: Left ventricular failure with pulmonary congestion
options.why: Failure lowers output steadily rather than in a respiratory pattern.

questions.stem: Match each structure in the conduction system to what it does.
questions.why: The impulse runs SA node → internodal pathways → AV node → bundle of His → bundle branches → Purkinje fibers. Knowing where an impulse originates tells you what its QRS should look like.
pairs: Sets the normal rate at 60 to 100
Delays the impulse so the ventricles can fill
Carries the impulse from the junction into the septum
Split the impulse toward the right and left ventricles
Spread the impulse through the ventricular walls
Move the impulse across the atria toward the junction

questions.stem: Match each term to the property of the heart it describes.
questions.why: The first three describe effects a drug or nerve can have on the heart. The last three describe properties the cardiac cells themselves possess.
pairs: Ability to respond to a stimulus
Ability to pass an impulse to neighboring cells

questions.stem: A patient has a stroke volume of 70 mL and a heart rate of 80. What is their cardiac output?
questions.why: Cardiac output equals stroke volume times heart rate: 70 mL × 80 = 5,600 mL, or 5.6 L/min — squarely in the normal adult range of 4 to 8.

options.t: 5.6 liters per minute
560 milliliters per minute
options.why: The arithmetic is right but the decimal is off by a factor of ten — 70 times 80 is 5,600 mL.

options.t: 150 milliliters per beat
options.why: That adds the two figures rather than multiplying them, and the units do not describe output.

options.t: 8.75 liters per minute
options.why: That divides rather than multiplies; output is stroke volume times rate.

questions.stem: What does an ejection fraction of 30 percent tell you?
questions.why: Ejection fraction is stroke volume divided by end-diastolic volume — normally 55 to 70 percent. At 30 percent the ventricle is keeping most of its volume each beat, the hallmark of systolic heart failure.

options.t: The heart is filling to only 30 percent of capacity
options.why: Filling is preload. Ejection fraction is about how much of what filled gets pushed out.

options.t: The patient's cardiac output is 30 percent of normal
options.why: Output can be held near normal by a faster rate or a dilated ventricle even with a poor fraction.

options.t: Only 30 percent of the myocardium is still viable
options.why: Ejection fraction measures pump performance, not how much muscle survived.

options.t: The ventricle is emptying poorly each beat

questions.stem: Which finding most strongly suggests that chest pain is cardiac rather than musculoskeletal?
questions.why: Exertional onset with relief at rest is the classic anginal pattern, because demand outstrips a fixed supply. None of these findings rules anything in or out on its own — atypical presentations are common, especially in women, diabetics and the elderly.

options.t: Pain that came on with exertion and eased with rest
Pain described as a sharp, well-localized point
options.why: A patient who can cover the spot with one fingertip is describing a pattern more typical of a chest wall origin.

options.t: Pain that changes with position and deep breathing
options.why: Positional, pleuritic pain suggests pericarditis or a pulmonary cause.

options.t: Pain that worsens sharply when the chest wall is pressed
options.why: Reproducible tenderness points toward the chest wall.
